newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA 96/97 FRUIT EXPORTS GROW, DESPITE WEATHER.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA 96/97 FRUIT EXPORTS GROW, DESPITE WEATHER.

text.p: South Africa's deciduous fruit marketer, Unifruco, said on Tuesday this season's export crop is expected to be 10 percent bigger than last season, smoothing fears of a hail and rain-damaged harvest.

Fred Meintjies, Unifruco's public relations manager, told Reuters although hailstorms had destroyed some fruit in the Langkloof area in the east of the country this had had little impact on total crop prospects.

"We are looking towards a (export) crop of around 55-million cartons in total of deciduous fruit. That would be an increase of about five-million cartons on last season," Meintjies said, adding that all fruits, bar nectarines, would be up on 1995/96. He said the 55-million carton forecast may be exceeded but that Unifruco preferred to provide conservative estimates.
The forecast exports comprised some six million cartons of stone fruit, which includes peaches, nectarines and apricots, 24 million cartons of grapes and 25 million of apples and pears.

Meintjies said the hail-damaged Langkloof area produced only around five percent of South Africa's total deciduous fruit harvest, and of that only 10 percent of the crop had been wiped out by recent storms.
"So although it is dramatic for those growers who have had hail, in total we still have very good crop prospects," he said.
Export fruit comprises on average 60-65 percent of South Africa's total crop, he said. Main markets include the European Union, the U.S. and the Middle East.
Unifruco said last month a late rainy winter season in the Western Cape province had affected the volumes of apricot, nectarine and peach produced for the export market.
But Meintjies said although the season was later than usual, fruit was now flowing onto the market.
"We are now into the swing of the harvest," he said.
